name: Nutritional yeast / B-vitamin loading

card.summary: Eating fortified yeast flakes or stacking B-complex for skin and hair; the vitamins are real, the cosmetic payoff is unstudied.
card.note: High-dose biotin can distort some lab test results.

quick.overview:
Nutritional yeast is a deactivated yeast eaten as a cheesy seasoning, and fortified versions contain large amounts of B vitamins. Some people in appearance communities use it or B-complex supplements hoping for better skin, hair and nails.

No clinical trial has tested the practice for cosmetic results. Evidence on individual vitamins such as biotin is limited in people who are not deficient.
quick.mechanism: B vitamins take part in normal skin and hair metabolism, and deficiency of some, such as biotin, can cause hair thinning, brittle nails or rash. Proponents extend this to the idea that extra intake improves appearance in people who are not deficient; that extension has not been tested in trials.
quick.risks: Nutritional yeast is a food and generally regarded as low risk. High-dose biotin supplements can interfere with some blood tests, including thyroid tests, per an FDA safety communication, and high niacin intake can cause flushing.

lead: Nutritional yeast, informally 'nooch', is a deactivated yeast, usually a strain of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, sold as yellow flakes, granules or powder and used in vegan cooking as a cheese-like seasoning.[1] In looksmaxxing and wider wellness circles, 'B-vitamin loading' means eating fortified nutritional yeast or taking B-complex supplements generously, with the aim of supporting skin, hair and nails from the inside.

The reasoning is that several B vitamins take part in skin, hair and nail biology and that deficiency can show up visibly. Biotin shortfall can cause hair thinning, brittle nails and a facial rash, and B12 deficiency is associated with skin colour changes, pale skin, hair loss and premature greying, according to encyclopedic sources.[2][3] Practitioners therefore treat a reliable, high intake of B vitamins as a base layer under a skin and hair routine.

Fortified nutritional yeast can supply several B vitamins far above the Daily Value per serving. Manufacturer figures reported on Wikipedia for one fortified brand list a 15 g serving as providing 992% of the Daily Value for thiamine, 754% for riboflavin, 288% for niacin, 347% for vitamin B6 and 733% for B12, alongside 8 g of protein and 60 kcal.[1] Yeast cannot make B12 itself, so the B12 in such products is added during fortification.[1] The Vegan Society lists fortified nutritional yeast among the foods many vegans use to raise B12 intake.[5]

chain: Eat fortified nutritional yeast or B-complex
Covers B-vitamin needs involved in skin, hair and nail upkeep
Healthier-looking skin, hair and nails, especially where intake had been low
angle.text: People who eat little animal food, or who simply want to cover their bases, use nutritional yeast as a high-B-vitamin, high-protein seasoning. The looks payoff is expected where a shortfall was affecting skin, hair or nails; for biotin and B12 deficiency, those visible signs are documented.

paras: Nutritional yeast is grown for several days on glucose from cane or beet molasses, then heat-killed, harvested, washed, dried and packaged.[1] Production strains are selected for traits that differ from baking and brewing strains.[1] Unlike yeast extract, which concentrates the water-soluble, umami-rich fraction, it is whole-cell, and unlike baker's yeast it is not used for leavening.[1] It has a nutty, cheesy flavour and is sprinkled on popcorn, potatoes and tofu or used as a cheese substitute.[1]

Manufacturer figures cited on Wikipedia for a fortified product also list 5 g of carbohydrate including 3 g of fibre and 0.5 g of fat per 15 g serving, with minerals low unless fortified.[1] B12 is commonly added as cyanocobalamin.[1]

The practice is discussed as part of nutrition-focused approaches to skin and hair, particularly among people who eat vegan or vegetarian diets. Vegans, and to a lesser degree vegetarians, are noted as at risk of low B12 unless they take supplements or eat fortified foods, which is one reason fortified yeast is popular.[3][5]

On bodybuilding forums such as T Nation, nutritional yeast comes up mostly as a seasoning, for example a cheesy popcorn topping suggested to other lifters.[6] 'Loading' in appearance circles usually means stacking fortified foods with a B-complex or biotin supplement as a baseline for skin and hair routines.

sections.h: What B-vitamin deficiency does to appearance
paras: Dietary biotin deficiency is rare, but subclinical deficiency may cause hair thinning, brittle fingernails or a facial skin rash.[2] Reviewers list causes of acquired deficiency including heavy raw egg white intake, certain anticonvulsants, isotretinoin, alcoholism and pregnancy, and inherited causes such as biotinidase deficiency.[4]

B12 deficiency is associated with skin colour changes including hyperpigmentation and dark circles under the eyes, pale skin and hair loss in moderate deficiency, premature greying, and a sore tongue with mouth ulcers or cracking at the mouth corners.[3] The Vegan Society says vegans can obtain B12 reliably only from fortified foods or supplements, and describes common deficiency signs as including a sore tongue, anaemia and fatigue.[5]

A 2010 review found two pre-1990 trials of 2.5 mg a day for several months, without placebo groups, that reported improved brittle nails.[2] A 2017 review in Skin Appendage Disorders identified 18 reported cases in which biotin was used for hair or nail changes; every patient had an underlying cause, such as an inherited enzyme deficiency, uncombable hair syndrome or brittle nail syndrome, and all improved. The authors found no randomized controlled trials showing benefit in healthy people and judged the evidence insufficient to support supplementation in healthy individuals.[4]

A letter responding to that review argued it had overlooked a study that found low biotin levels in 38 percent of women with hair loss and that biotin assessment may be advisable in such patients; the review's authors regarded that study as confounded.[4] A 2018 meta-review described results for several nail conditions as promising.[2]

A 28 November 2017 FDA safety communication warned that high-dose biotin, with intakes of 5 mg a day or more as the stated risk level, can interfere with biotin-streptavidin laboratory tests such as thyroid hormone and 25-hydroxyvitamin D assays, giving falsely normal or abnormal results; patients may need to stop supplements for 48 hours or longer before testing.[2] The US National Academy of Medicine and EFSA have not set an upper intake limit for biotin because adverse effects of high intake have not been established.[2] The 2017 review likewise reports that no major toxicities of excess biotin have been described.[4]
Folic acid can mask the anaemia of B12 deficiency while nerve damage continues.[3] The Vegan Society advises anyone who suspects a B12 deficiency to consult a health professional.[5]
No studies found on nutritional yeast or broad B-vitamin loading for appearance. Studies of biotin alone are summarised above.[2][4]

timeline.event: Review notes two older uncontrolled trials reporting improved brittle nails with biotin.[2]
Skin Appendage Disorders review finds 18 case reports of biotin benefit, all with underlying causes, and no trials in healthy people.[4]
FDA issues a safety communication on biotin interference with laboratory tests (28 November).[2]

lore.intro: Nutritional yeast is discussed in fitness and appearance forums mainly as a cheesy, protein-rich seasoning, with B-vitamin stacking mentioned as a skin and hair baseline.[6]

claims.claim: Extra B vitamins improve skin, hair and nails.
claims.believers: Proponents point to documented hair, nail and skin changes in biotin and B12 deficiency and extend the logic to higher intake.[2][3]
claims.experts: A 2017 review found benefit in reported cases with underlying causes and no randomized trials in healthy people.[4]

claims.claim: Fortified nutritional yeast is a dependable B12 source for people eating no animal foods.
claims.believers: Vegans use it as a flavourful way to raise B12 intake.[5]
claims.experts: The Vegan Society lists fortified nutritional yeast among usable sources, and Wikipedia notes that yeast cannot make B12 so it must be added.[1][5]

claims.believers: Reviews note that no major toxicities have been reported and no upper limit has been set.[2][4]
claims.experts: The FDA warned in 2017 that intakes of 5 mg a day or more can distort some lab test results.[2]
